text: Next, we discuss the results from the execution of Scenario 2 on the Vulcan test platform. We show four plots in each figure, plot (a) shows the grid voltage and plot (b) shows the power from energy sources (utility, BESS, Generators and UPS). In plot (c) the average SOC of the BESS units are shown and plot (d) shows the total IT and cooling load. The initial state of the power system is grid-connected mode with 100% of the load supported with power from the grid, as shown in Figure 5 (a), when time t < 180 second. The BESS and the generator aggre- gate output is zero, and the SOC of the BESS is flat (because it is not discharging). Around 180 second mark, we simulate a voltage sag event and drop the grid voltage from 230 kV to 2 kV as shown in Figure 15 This report is available at no cost from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) at www.nrel.gov/publications 5 (a). The PFMS detects its islanding criteria to be met, and it executes the islanding process (see Algo- rithm 3). As shown in Figure 5, between t =180 and t =210, the power from the grid drops to zero after the utility breaker is opened by the PFMS. At this stage, there are no energy sources powering the power system, and the IT load is supported by the UPS. Next, PFMS uses the BESS units in GFM mode to pro- vide backup power to the IT and cooling loads, as confirmed by the BESS output power in the Figure 5 (b) after t =210 seconds. The average SOC of the BESS units start to decrease. Overall, it took less than 30 seconds to island the 70 MW power system after detecting the unstable grid conditions. The power system continues to operate in off grid/ islanded mode with backup power provided by the BESS units. In Figure 6, as the SOC of the BESS drops below the threshold of 50 %(SOC ), the PFMS LS alerts the IT workload owner (via communication interfaces such as OpenADR) to consider shedding the low-priority/interruptible workloads to extend the run time of the BESS (Algorithm 4). We simulate a load shed around t∼940 second by using a multiplier of M=0.7, as shown in Figure 6 (d). The load drops from approximately ∼45 MW to ∼35 MW, and the SOC curve of the BESS units shows the slowdown of the BESS depletion through the change of slope around the inflection point (just after the t ∼940 second mark). Figure 7 shows the runtime remaining on the BESS increases by about 30 % due to shedding of interruptible workloads. Here, the runtime remaining is computed using a ratio of the remaining energy in the BESS units (based on average SOC of the units) to the last 5 second average load. As the SOC of the BESS units drop further and reaches below the minimum SOC threshold of 15%(SOC ), L the PFMS brings online an appropriate number of generators to support the load (Algorithm 4).
